content_record.title: Botanical Compounds Engage Interlocking Cellular Networks to Shield Aging Neurons
content_record.editorial_body: Multi-omics analysis reveals how plant molecules modify key regulatory proteins, maintain mitochondrial power grids, and reshape chromatin to halt systems-level neuronal decay. Neurodegenerative conditions like Alzheimer's and Parkinson's do not spring from a single broken protein gear. They mark a widespread structural collapse across multiple interconnected cellular support systems. For decades, drug discovery focused on solitary molecular targets, designing synthetic compounds to block individual enzymes or clear isolated amyloid sheets. Yet these single-key drugs consistently fall short in clinical trials, briefly masking symptoms while the underlying neural scaffold continues to disintegrate. The failure lies in the interconnected nature of neuronal destruction. Inside an aging neuron, radical oxygen ions strip electrons from cell membranes, altering structural lipids and damaging metabolic machinery. These oxidized lipids and damaged proteins strain the mitochondria, which leak electrons, spill toxic hydrogen peroxide into the cytoplasm, and lose their capacity to generate ATP. Simultaneously, reactive astrocytes and microglial cells release inflammatory cytokines, while clogged proteasomes fail to digest misfolded protein aggregates. Because each mechanical breakdown accelerates the next, disabling a single downstream enzyme cannot halt the broader structural collapse. Synthesizing over a decade of transcriptomic sequencing, mass spectrometry proteomics, metabolomic profiling, and epigenome mapping reveals how plant-derived compounds interact with complex cellular networks. Rather than binding exclusively to a single active site like targeted pharmaceuticals, neuroactive phytochemicals—including berberine, curcumin, ginsenosides, quercetin, and resveratrol—exert broad biological effects. These molecules act simultaneously across distinct cellular compartments to maintain structural integrity. By cross-referencing multi-omics datasets with historical ethnopharmacology from Ayurveda, Traditional Chinese Medicine, and Amazonian botanical records, researchers tracked how plant molecules alter mRNA transcription and protein phosphorylation across full metabolic pathways. Rather than forcing a single isolated reaction, these complex botanical mixtures tune central signaling nodes. This multi-point regulation helps preserve dendritic spine architecture and maintain synaptic vesicle cycling under sustained oxidative stress. At the physical interface of the cell, plant compounds engage specific protein switches that govern survival circuits. A primary site of action is the Nrf2-Keap1 complex, which controls endogenous antioxidant production. Under baseline conditions, the sensor protein Keap1 holds Nrf2 in the cytoplasm for ubiquitin-tagged destruction. Plant electrophiles directly modify critical cysteine thiol groups on Keap1, changing its shape so Nrf2 can break free and enter the nucleus. Once inside, Nrf2 docks onto antioxidant response elements in the DNA, driving the transcription of protective enzymes like heme oxygenase-1 and NQO1 that neutralize free radicals. Concurrently, these compounds prevent the phosphorylation of IκB, keeping the NF-κB transcription factor trapped in the cytoplasm and silencing inflammatory gene expression. This dual mechanism stabilizes mitochondrial membranes, promoting the selective engulfment of damaged mitochondria through mitophagy while activating PGC-1α to build new metabolic machinery. Epigenetically, plant molecules inhibit histone deacetylases and alter DNA methyltransferase activity, keeping tightly wound chromatin open so survival genes remain accessible. This systemic control aligns with the bioenergetic framework established by Douglas C. Wallace, who demonstrated that age-related neurodegeneration stems from progressive decay in mitochondrial electron transport. Phytochemicals reinforce this core cellular power grid. Translating these biochemical mechanisms into effective human medicines requires overcoming major physiological barriers. Many hydrophobic phytochemicals face poor intestinal absorption, rapid glucuronidation in the liver, and exclusion by P-glycoprotein efflux pumps at the blood-brain barrier, preventing effective concentrations from reaching central neurons. Furthermore, standard laboratory models, such as flat immortalized cell cultures, lack the three-dimensional architecture, metabolic gradient, and specialized glial interactions of the aging human brain. As a result, promising molecular interventions in petri dishes often fail inside complex human tissue. Overcoming these limits demands standardized cultivation and extraction processes to ensure consistent molecular ratios, paired with advanced delivery vehicles like solid lipid nanoparticles that cross the brain's microvasculature. Notably, surrogate systemic markers, such as blood-based DNA methylation clocks, cannot directly confirm tissue-specific anti-inflammatory signaling, localized mitochondrial repair, or structural synaptic preservation in the brain. Until clinical trials evaluate stabilized, brain-permeable formulations, these multi-omics maps serve as blueprints for network-based drug design rather than immediate off-the-shelf cures. Neurodegeneration arises from compounded failures in lipid peroxidation control, mitochondrial electron transport, glial inflammatory cascades, and lysosomal debris clearance. Molecules such as berberine and curcumin covalently alter Keap1 cysteine residues to trigger Nrf2 nuclear translocation while simultaneously blocking NF-κB nuclear entry. Clinical application remains constrained by rapid phase II liver metabolism, poor intestinal transport, and restricted clearance across the blood-brain barrier microvasculature. Reported from Medicinal plants as neuroprotective agents: multi-omics and epigenetic insights from ethnopharmacology (Frontiers in Pharmacology (Ethnopharmacology & Botanicals)).
